how_to_read: Seven more deposit stories (deposit-6 to deposit-12), in the same shape as stories.json. Each runs on lease.txt unless it has a 'lease' field, which names a copy of lease.txt in this folder with only what the story needs changed: lease_email.txt (clause 8: a signed e-mail addendum), lease_monthtomonth.txt (clauses 3 and 9: month to month), lease_school.txt (new clause 11: enrollment), lease_fee.txt (clause 5: a fee instead of a deposit). 'today' is the date count_days compares with in that story. 'facts' are the confirmed facts the record holds (count_days reads the dates). 'message' is what the tenant writes. 'answer' is the right answer in plain words; 'points' are what a right answer must convey, judged by meaning (words in parentheses are helpful detail, not required); 'mistakes' make an answer wrong. 'law' quotes the statute words each point rests on, word for word from statutes/, with the subsection they sit in. 'dates' are the count_days results the answer needs. Two notes. In deposit-9 the statute does not say which date ends the rental agreement when a tenant leaves early, so the key requires both readings. In deposit-12, 83.491(6) points to 83.43(13) for the meaning of 'security deposit', but in the stored 83.43, (13) is 'Rental agreement' and 'Security deposits' is (14); the key quotes 83.491(6) as it stands. Check the key with: python check_key.py stories_more.json

stories.title: A certified notice of claim, still time to object

facts.forwarding_address: given in writing, mailed to the office on 2026-07-28
facts.landlord_notice_of_claim: a letter dated 2026-08-20, sent by certified mail to the forwarding address and signed for by the tenant on 2026-08-24; it says the landlord is keeping $400 for carpet replacement, tells the tenant to object in writing within 15 days, and gives the office address to send the objection to

stories.message: My lease ended July 31 and I moved out that day. I'd mailed them my new address. On August 24 I signed for a certified letter dated August 20. It says they're keeping $400 of my $1,050 deposit to replace the carpet. I think the carpet was just worn from normal use. What can I do, and when do I get the other $650?
stories.answer: The landlord has not lost the right to make this claim: a letter by certified mail that gives the amount and the reason is the notice the statute asks for, and this one is dated 2026-08-20, before the 30 days after the lease ended run out on 2026-08-30 (from count_days). You can object, in writing, within 15 days after you received it. Your last day is 2026-09-08 (from count_days, counting from August 24), and that has not passed. Unless you object, the landlord may deduct the $400 and must send you the balance, $650, within 30 days after the date of the notice, which is 2026-09-19 (from count_days, counting from August 20); that has not passed either. Send the objection to the address in the letter. The statute does not say what happens after you object, other than that either side can go to court over the deposit, and the winner gets court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee.
points: The notice by certified mail is the kind the statute requires, so the landlord has not forfeited the right to make the claim; this is not the whole-deposit case. (The notice is dated 2026-08-20, before the 30 days after the lease ended run out on 2026-08-30, from count_days.)
The tenant can object, in writing, within 15 days after receiving the notice; the last day is 2026-09-08 (count_days from the date received), and it has not passed.
Unless the tenant objects, the landlord may deduct the $400, and must send the balance within 30 days after the date of the notice: 2026-09-19 (count_days from the date of the notice), not passed.

(If the tenant objects, the statute sets no step after that except a court action, so what follows is not settled. If someone goes to court over the deposit, the winner gets court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee.)
mistakes: Says the landlord forfeited the deposit or must return all $1,050.
Counts the 15 days from the date on the letter instead of the day the tenant received it, or the 30 days from the day received instead of the date of the notice.

Says what follows an objection as if the statute settled it (the claim is cancelled, or the landlord may deduct anyway); the statute says only that without a timely objection the landlord may deduct, and it names a court action.
Gives a date it worked out itself instead of from count_days.

law.quote: If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim.
you must object in writing to this deduction from your security deposit within 15 days after the time you receive this notice

Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages.

If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney.

stories.title: A notice came, no objection, no balance sent

facts.forwarding_address: given in writing, mailed to the office on 2026-07-28
facts.landlord_notice_of_claim: a letter dated 2026-08-20, sent by certified mail to the forwarding address and signed for by the tenant on 2026-08-24; it says the landlord is keeping $400 for carpet replacement, tells the tenant to object in writing within 15 days, and gives the office address to send the objection to

stories.message: My lease ended July 31 and I moved out that day. On August 24 I signed for a certified letter dated August 20 saying they're keeping $400 of my $1,050 deposit for the carpet. I never wrote back. I figured I'd lose anyway. It's been almost two months and they never sent me the other $650. Do they have to? And is the $400 just gone because I didn't object?
stories.answer: Yes, the $650 is overdue. The notice came by certified mail, so it was proper, and the landlord had to send the balance within 30 days after the date of the notice. That date (2026-09-19, from count_days) has passed with no money. About the $400: your 15 days to object ran out on 2026-09-08 (from count_days, counting from the day you received the letter), so the landlord may deduct it. But not objecting does not take away your right to seek damages in a separate action; the statute's own notice to tenants calls that a lawsuit claiming a refund. If either side sues over the deposit, the winner gets court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee.
points: The $650 balance is overdue: the landlord had to send it within 30 days after the date of the notice, 2026-09-19 (count_days from the date of the notice), and that has passed.

The notice was proper (certified mail) and the tenant did not object within 15 days after receiving it (last day 2026-09-08, count_days from the date received, passed), so the landlord may deduct the $400.
Not objecting does not waive the tenant's rights to seek damages in a separate action (a lawsuit claiming a refund).
(If someone sues over the deposit, the winner gets court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee.)

Says the tenant lost the right to the $400 for good because they did not object.
Says the $650 is not yet due.

Gives a date it worked out itself instead of from count_days.

Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages.

stories.title: The claim came by e-mail, with a signed e-mail addendum

facts.forwarding_address: given in writing, mailed to the office on 2026-07-28
facts.email_addendum: signed by the tenant and the landlord on 2025-07-10, with an e-mail address for each
facts.landlord_notice_of_claim: an e-mail sent on 2026-08-20 to the tenant's e-mail address in the addendum and read by the tenant that day; it says the landlord is keeping $400 for carpet replacement, tells the tenant to object in writing within 15 days, and gives the office address to send the objection to; nothing by certified mail

stories.message: My lease ended July 31 and I moved out that day. I'd mailed them my new address. On August 20 the manager e-mailed me that they're keeping $400 of my $1,050 deposit to replace the carpet, and I read it that day. Nothing came in the mail, no certified letter. When I moved in, we both signed something about using e-mail for notices. Can I just ignore the e-mail since it wasn't certified mail? I don't think the carpet was my fault.
stories.answer: No, you should not ignore it. The e-mail counts. The statute lets the landlord give the notice of a claim by e-mail when both of you have signed an addendum agreeing to e-mail notices, and you did sign one (your lease says so). The e-mail is dated 2026-08-20, before the 30 days after the lease ended run out on 2026-08-30 (from count_days), so the landlord has not lost the right to make the claim. You can object, in writing, within 15 days after you received it. Your last day is 2026-09-04 (from count_days, counting from August 20), and that has not passed, so do it soon. Unless you object, the landlord may deduct the $400 and must send you the balance, $650, within 30 days after the date of the notice, which is 2026-09-19 (from count_days). Not objecting would not take away your right to seek damages in a separate action.
points: The e-mail is a proper notice of a claim: the statute allows notice by e-mail when the parties signed an addendum agreeing to it, and they did (the lease and the facts say so). So it counts even though it did not come by certified mail, and the tenant should not ignore it. The answer does not treat this as an open question.
The landlord has not forfeited the right to make the claim: the notice came before the 30 days after the lease ended run out on 2026-08-30 (count_days).
The tenant can object, in writing, within 15 days after receiving it; the last day is 2026-09-04 (count_days from the date received), and it has not passed.
Unless the tenant objects, the landlord may deduct the $400, and must send the balance within 30 days after the date of the notice: 2026-09-19 (count_days from the date of the notice), not passed.
(Not objecting does not waive the tenant's right to seek damages in a separate action.)
mistakes: Says the e-mail does not count because it did not come by certified mail.
Gives two readings of whether the e-mail counts, as if it were an open question; with a signed addendum it counts.
Says the landlord forfeited the deposit or must return all $1,050.
Says what follows an objection as if the statute settled it; the statute names only a court action.
Gives a date it worked out itself instead of from count_days.

stories.title: Left early with the right notice: which date counts

facts.notice_before_leaving: a letter sent by certified mail to the office on 2026-06-01 and signed for there on 2026-06-03, saying the tenant would be out on 2026-06-15 and giving the tenant's new address

stories.message: I got a job in Tampa and moved out on June 15, about six weeks before my lease ended on July 31. On June 1 I sent the office a letter by certified mail saying I'd be out on the 15th, with my new address in it. It's August 10 and I haven't heard a word about my $1,050 deposit. The landlord hasn't sent me any notice. Do they have to give it all back?
stories.answer: That depends on a point the statute does not settle, so here are both readings. Your notice before leaving was the right kind (certified mail, at least 7 days before you left, with your address; the last day for it was 2026-06-08, from count_days), so the landlord is not relieved of the duty to send a notice of a claim, and none came. The open question is which date ends the rental agreement when a tenant leaves early: the day you moved out, or the day the lease ended. If it is the day you moved out (2026-06-15), the landlord's 30 days ended 2026-07-15 (from count_days). That has passed, so the landlord forfeited the right to impose a claim and must return the whole $1,050, though it may still sue for damages after returning it. If it is the day the lease ended (2026-07-31), the 30 days end 2026-08-30 (from count_days). That has not passed, so the landlord can still send a notice of a claim by certified mail until then, and nothing is forfeited yet. Your lease does not set a different rule on notice before leaving early.
points: The tenant's notice (certified mail, with an address, at least 7 days before leaving; the last day was 2026-06-08 from count_days) meets the early-leaving rule, so the landlord was not relieved of the notice of a claim.
Which date ends the rental agreement for a tenant who leaves early, move-out or lease end, is not settled; the answer gives both readings and chooses neither.

Move-out reading: 30 days after move_out_date is 2026-07-15 (count_days), passed; no notice came, so the landlord forfeited and must return the whole $1,050 (and may still sue for damages after returning it).
Lease-end reading: 30 days after lease_end_date is 2026-08-30 (count_days), not passed; the landlord can still send a notice of a claim by certified mail, so nothing is forfeited yet.
mistakes: Takes one date as settled, saying flatly that the landlord has forfeited or flatly that it has not.
Gives only one of the two readings, or only one count_days result.
Says the landlord is relieved of the notice requirement, or that the tenant lost the right to the deposit, because the tenant left early; the tenant gave the right notice.
Gives a date it worked out itself instead of from count_days.

law.quote: Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement

must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached

If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim.
Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement
WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT

If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant.

stories.title: Month to month, told the manager out loud

facts.notice_before_leaving: told the manager face to face at the office on 2026-07-20 that the tenant would be out on 2026-08-31; nothing in writing; nothing by certified mail
facts.forwarding_address: given in writing, handed to the office on 2026-08-31

stories.message: I rent month to month. On July 20 I told the manager at the office that I'd be out on August 31, and I moved out that day. I never wrote anything down. Seven weeks later I still haven't heard anything about my $1,050 deposit, and the landlord never sent me any notice. Don't they have to give it all back now?
stories.answer: Not for that reason. You rented month to month, and the statute says a tenant who leaves a month-to-month tenancy must give the landlord at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where you can be reached. Telling the manager out loud is not written notice. Without that notice, the landlord is relieved of the 30-day notice requirement, so the landlord's silence does not forfeit any claim, even though the 30 days after the tenancy ended (2026-09-30, from count_days) have passed. You have not lost your right to the deposit, though: the statute says so in the same sentence. Your lease does not set a different rule on notice before leaving.
points: No, the landlord's silence does not forfeit its claim here, because a tenant who leaves a month-to-month tenancy must give 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery with an address, and a spoken notice is not that; without it the landlord is relieved of the notice requirement.
The tenant has not lost the right to the deposit or any part of it.
(The 30 days after the tenancy ended passed on 2026-09-30, from count_days, but that does not change the answer.)
mistakes: Says the landlord forfeited the right to keep any of the deposit, for example because the 30 days passed.
Says the tenant lost all right to the deposit.
Says a month-to-month tenant does not need to give notice before leaving.
Says the lease provides otherwise on notice before leaving (it does not).
Gives a date it worked out itself instead of from count_days.

law.quote: any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year

must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached
Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it.

stories.message: I moved out on July 31 when my lease ended. I mailed my new address to the office before I left. It's been over two months and my landlord hasn't returned my $1,050 deposit or told me anything. Can I get all of it back?
stories.answer: I can't answer that yet, because I first need to know whether this part of the law covers your housing. It leaves out living in a facility when the living there is incidental to educational or similar services, and your lease ties the apartment to school: you must be enrolled at Alachua Valley College, and the landlord may end the lease if you are not. The lease alone does not settle it. So, one question: is your housing run by or for your school, or can you live there only while you are enrolled? (Once I know, I can tell you where the deposit stands. If this part of the law does apply, no notice of a claim came within 30 days after the lease ended, and that date (2026-08-30, from count_days) has passed, so the rules would give you all $1,050 back.)

stories.title: A fee paid instead of a deposit

facts.fee: $350 paid on 2025-07-10 instead of a security deposit; no security deposit was paid
facts.fee_agreement: signed by the landlord and the tenant on 2025-07-10; it and the lease both call the fee nonrefundable
facts.forwarding_address: given in writing, mailed to the office on 2026-07-28

stories.message: When I moved in, I paid a $350 fee instead of a security deposit. I moved out July 31 when my lease ended and left the place clean. It's been over two months and the landlord hasn't sent me anything or given back the $350. The lease calls it nonrefundable, but they never sent me any notice about keeping it. Isn't it like a deposit they have to return?
stories.answer: Not as a deposit. The statute says a fee paid in place of a security deposit is not a security deposit, so the deposit rules in 83.49 (all of it back if no notice of a claim comes within 30 days) are not what decides this $350. Whether any of the fee comes back turns on your written fee agreement and lease, and both call it nonrefundable. The statute has the landlord tell the tenant in writing that the fee is nonrefundable, if that applies, and that the fee is only for securing occupancy without paying a required security deposit. So the landlord's silence does not make the landlord owe you the $350.
points: The $350 is a fee paid in place of a security deposit, and the statute says such a fee is not a security deposit; so the deposit rules in 83.49 (return in 15 days, a notice of a claim within 30 days, forfeiture) are not what decides this money.
The landlord's silence does not mean the tenant gets the fee back as if a deposit were forfeited.

Whether the fee comes back turns on the written fee agreement and the lease, which here call it nonrefundable; the statute has the landlord tell the tenant in writing that the fee is nonrefundable, if that applies.
mistakes: Treats the fee as a security deposit, or says the landlord forfeited it by sending no notice of a claim within 30 days.
Says the tenant is owed the $350 back under 83.49.
Says the fee must be refunded, or the fee agreement is void, because of a missing term or notice under 83.491; the statute's words say no such result.

law.quote: A fee collected under this section, or an insurance product or a surety bond accepted, by a landlord in lieu of a security deposit is not a security deposit as defined in s. 83.43 (13).
